# Abstract

This gazetteer compiles coordinates, spatial scopes and multi-period population series for 1.763 individually assessed urban and rural settlements across Modern Southern Africa between 1902AD and 2026AD. Screened from 2.508 candidate places (745 duplicate alias records and overlapping boundary shells excluded), the retained entries span 11.016 chronological observations across South Africa (1.232), Namibia (94), Botswana (70), Lesotho (48), Eswatini (33) and 22 cross-border buffer towns in Mozambique, Angola, Zambia and Zimbabwe. Active interpolated entries rise from 850 centres in 1910AD to 1.008 in 1952AD, 1.019 in 1970AD, 1.065 in 1995AD and 664 by 2025AD, led by the metropolitan agglomerations of Johannesburg (11,01M), Cape Town (4,39M), Durban (3,52M), Maputo (2,98M), Windhoek (566,2k), Gaborone (534,8k), Maseru (505,7k) and Manzini (328,9k).



# Background

Compiling a unified twentieth- and early twenty-first-century settlement gazetteer for Southern Africa requires reconciling disparate colonial, Apartheid and post-colonial enumeration traditions [@Caldwell2002HistoricalPopulation; @ChimereDan2013ApartheidAnd]. Union and Republic censuses in South Africa separated European municipal boroughs from segregated townships and ethnic Bantustans between 1911AD and 1991AD, whereas post-1994AD wall-to-wall municipalities merged suburban cores and outlying settlements into single metropolitan jurisdictions [@Simkins2011SouthAfrica; @Bakker2020MigrationAnd]. Neighbouring statistical agencies in Namibia, Botswana, Lesotho and Eswatini similarly transitioned from colonial district headcounts to modern geocoded village and town registers [@StatsSA2023Census2022; @NSA2024NamibiaCensus; @StatsBotswana2022Census].

# Methodology

## Candidate Screening and Territorial Accounting

Candidate settlements were screened from official census tables, OECD/SWAC Africapolis urban polygons, UNSD Demographic Yearbook series and historical statistical registers [@StatsSA2023Census2022; @Deleu2015ImprovingAfripop]. Across the 2.671.510 km² study domain bounded over geoBoundaries administrative outlines [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries], 745 duplicate alias records were removed, leaving 1.763 retained settlements across 11.016 observations. Of those entries, 1.477 fall inside the five core sovereign territories (1.487 interior cell matches across the 46 Admin-1 sub-regions plus coastal or frontier edge matches) and 22 lie in adjacent border corridors of Mozambique, Angola, Zambia and Zimbabwe to anchor cross-frontier interpolation.

## Scope Classification and Benchmark Interpolation

Every settlement carries an explicit spatial scope distinguishing 1.742 city-proper places from 21 metropolitan agglomerations, preventing municipal cores and encompassing urban footprints from being conflated [@Bakker2020MigrationAnd]. Tables \ref{tab:zaf-t1} through \ref{tab:buf-sites} list all 1.763 settlements partitioned by country and South African peak-population tier, reporting linearly interpolated populations at 1910AD, 1952AD, 1970AD, 1995AD and 2025AD alongside each settlement's observed peak population and peak year. Dates preceding foundation or earliest census attestation and dates after municipal absorption or boundary discontinuation appear as hyphens (-).

# Testing and Validation

Across all 1.763 settlements, rank-size regression yields $q = 0,98$ ($R^2 = 0,9922$) across the upper 180 urban centres and $q = 1,40$ ($R^2 = 0,8893$) across the full ledger, matching the 1.414 spatially deduplicated settlement peaks ($q = 0,99$, $R^2 = 0,99$) plotted in Figure \ref{fig:settlements-rank}. Chronological and coordinate screening eliminates duplicate urban synonyms and checks alignment between historical boundary transitions and municipal census dates [@Udjo2014EstimatingDemographic; @Mkhatha2024ResponseMoultrie].

# Results

## South Africa: Tier 1 Metropolitan Agglomerations and Major Cities (92 Sites)

Table \ref{tab:zaf-t1} records the 92 largest South African centres reaching 100k or more inhabitants at peak, led by the Johannesburg agglomeration (11,01M), Cape Town agglomeration (4,39M), Durban agglomeration (3,52M), Soshanguve (1,91M), Pretoria agglomeration (1,76M), Evaton (1,09M) and Port Elizabeth (957,3k) [@StatsSA2023Census2022; @Simkins2011SouthAfrica].

## South Africa: Tier 2 Secondary Cities (199 Sites)

Table \ref{tab:zaf-t2} catalogues 201 secondary South African cities and industrial towns peaking between 30k and 100k inhabitants, spanning provincial service centres, mining municipalities and peri-urban growth corridors across all nine provinces [@Bakker2020MigrationAnd; @Africa2024ProvincialProfile].

<figure class="crd-table-figure" id="tab:zaf-t2">

# Limitations

Three caveats govern this settlement ledger. First, individual place series terminate or shift scope when municipal boundaries are amalgamated, meaning pre-2000AD city-proper entries and post-2000AD metropolitan agglomerations appear as separate rows to prevent artificial leaps [@Bakker2020MigrationAnd]. Second, interpolated benchmark columns display a hyphen outside each settlement's attested span, so settlements founded after 1952AD (such as Gaborone in 1964AD or Secunda in the 1970s) show blanks at earlier benchmarks. Third, summing raw rows across both city-proper and metropolitan entries double-counts overlapping urban cores and should never substitute for the 46-polygon regional totals in the companion literature review.

# Conclusion

Together, the 1.763 settlements catalogued in Tables \ref{tab:zaf-t1} through \ref{tab:buf-sites} trace Southern Africa's urban transformation from 1902AD colonial mining and port nodes to contemporary metropolitan corridors, anchoring both sub-national disaggregation and rank-size calibration across all five sovereign states.
